strengths: Addresses an underexplored niche—combining learned optimization with second-order (SR1) quasi-Newton structure—rather than the more commonly studied first-order learned optimizers.

The limited-memory, buffer-based rank-one construction (Eq. 7) is a sensible way to keep the learned preconditioner PSD by construction while retaining scalability across problem dimensions, and the element-wise MLP design gives dimension invariance, which is empirically tested by training on small N and testing on larger N.

Reasonably broad experimental suite: controlled quadratic ablations isolating the effect of the projection term, performance-profile comparisons against LBFGS/Adam/AdaHessian on a battery of benchmark functions, and a real downstream application (HMR on 3DPW).

Good engineering transparency: detailed appendices with architecture tables, hyperparameters, ablations on encoder inputs/hidden size, and runtime/memory profiling, which aids reproducibility even though code is not yet released.

The HMR results show a smaller model (10.4M vs 17.4M parameters) reaching lower PA-MPJPE than the LGD baseline without task-specific fine-tuning, which is a meaningful practical selling point if the efficiency claims hold up.
weaknesses: The central 'learned projection' is somewhat misleadingly named: Eq. (8) is not an operator applied at inference to project a candidate matrix onto the PSD/secant-consistent set; rather it is a soft penalty term (Rsec) added to the meta-training loss that shapes the vector generator's outputs. This is fine as a design choice, but calling it a 'projection' and claiming it ensures 'theoretical soundness' and 'preserves core Quasi-Newton properties' overstates the guarantee—satisfaction of the secant condition is only approximate and only encouraged during training, not enforced at test time.

The efficiency narrative is internally inconsistent: Table 1 shows L-SR1 needs 13 inner iterations to reach its best PA-MPJPE versus 4 for LGD, while Table 2 reports per-iteration runtime (91ms vs 166ms). Multiplying these out, L-SR1's total inference time (~1.18s) is actually about 1.8x longer than LGD's (~0.66s) to reach its reported best result, which directly contradicts the paper's repeated claims of 'faster convergence' and is never discussed or reconciled in the text.

HMR evaluation includes only one learned-optimization baseline (LGD); stronger or more recent second-order-inspired learned optimizers cited in related work (e.g., Gärtner et al.'s transformer-based optimizer, Ayad et al.'s unrolled BFGS) are discussed qualitatively but not compared quantitatively, weakening the claim of outperforming 'existing learned optimization-based approaches.'

Analytic experiments are conducted at fairly small scale (training at N=2 for quadratics, N=100 for performance profiles) with modest test sets (30–32 problems), and no variance across multiple random seeds/training runs is reported for the main comparison plots (Fig. 3), making it hard to assess statistical robustness of the reported gains.
Notational inconsistency between the main paper (pk = xk − xk−1) and the appendix (pk = xk+1 − xk) for the secant-pair definitions could confuse readers trying to reproduce the method exactly.
Code is not yet released ('will be made publicly available'), so full reproducibility currently rests solely on the appendix descriptions.

The theoretical content (Lemma 1, positive-definiteness needed for descent direction) is standard textbook material restated rather than a new theoretical contribution, so the paper's claimed 'theoretical soundness' rests more on architectural design than new analysis.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely underexplored niche—combining learned optimization with second-order (SR1) quasi-Newton updates—and proposes a reasonably motivated architecture (encoder, vector generator, learning-rate generator) that maintains dimension-invariance through element-wise operation.

The limited-memory buffer construction (Eq. 7) that guarantees PSD-ness of the reconstructed preconditioner as long as B0 ⊕ 0 is a sensible and cheap way to sidestep SR1's classical lack of PSD guarantees.

Evaluation spans both controlled analytic benchmarks (quadratics, Rosenbrock, Rastrigin, performance profiles) and a real downstream vision task (HMR on 3DPW), giving some breadth to the empirical claims.
The HMR integration shows a smaller model size (10.4M vs 17.4M parameters) and lower measured runtime/memory than the LGD baseline (Table 2), which is a useful practical point if it generalizes.
Ablation studies (Appendix B) on encoder inputs and hidden dimension are provided, showing some care was taken in the design process.
weaknesses: The central claim of the abstract/intro that the method 'requires no annotated data' and is trained 'in a self-supervised manner' directly contradicts the meta-loss in Eq. 13 for the HMR experiments, which explicitly includes a supervised term λself∥Θk − Θgt∥1 using ground-truth SMPL parameters from AMASS. This is a substantive misrepresentation of the training setup that undermines a key selling point of the paper.

The 'learned projection' (Section 4.2) is not actually a projection performed at inference time; it is merely a soft penalty term added to the meta-training loss (Eq. 9). Calling this operation a 'projection' that 'maintains positive semi-definiteness... via a learned projection' (as stated in the abstract) is misleading, since the constrained form in Eq. 7 already guarantees PSD-ness independent of whether the secant penalty is used, and the penalty itself only approximately (not exactly) enforces the secant condition during training, with no guarantee at test time.

The analytic experiments use extremely low-dimensional problems for meta-training (N=2) with only modest dimension transfer to N=10 for testing in Section 5.1.1, which is a weak test of the claimed dimension-invariance/generalization; the performance-profile experiment (Section 5.1.2) trains three separate models per task family and it is unclear which model is used at test time for each of the 30 combined problems, making the setup ambiguous and hard to reproduce.

The HMR comparison in Table 1 is limited to SMPLify, SPIN, and LGD, omitting several more recent and directly relevant methods discussed in the related work (e.g., WHAM, PLIKS, TRACE, PromptHMR), and no error bars, statistical significance, or multiple-seed results are reported for the single headline PA-MPJPE number (51.58), making it hard to assess robustness of the reported improvement.

LBFGS is used as an 'oracle-like' baseline in Fig. 4/Table-adjacent discussion for HMR (initialized with the paper's own trained initialization module), but it is unclear whether LBFGS's step size / line search was tuned fairly against the learned method, and the paper does not report LBFGS as a numeric baseline in Table 1, weakening the comparison's completeness.

The buffer-based construction in Eq. 7, which sums L rank-one outer products, is structurally closer to a low-rank (L-BFGS-style) approximation than to the classical single rank-one SR1 update; framing the entire contribution as an extension of 'SR1' specifically (rather than a generic low-rank PSD preconditioner) somewhat overstates the connection to the named classical method.

Presentation issues remain: Algorithm 1 initializes d0 ← g0 without justification/sign convention consistency with the update rule in line 11 (which subtracts αk ⊙ dk), and several figures (e.g., Fig. 3b, Fig. 8) are referenced with limited explanation of axis meaning or specific take-aways in the main text, relegating essential details (hyperparameters, encoder details) entirely to a lengthy appendix that a reader must cross-reference to evaluate reproducibility.

No wall-clock or iteration-count comparison against a strong non-learned second-order baseline (e.g., true LBFGS with line search) is given in the main HMR results table, despite LBFGS appearing in the trajectory figures; this omission makes it hard to judge whether the learned model provides real net benefit over simple, well-tuned classical alternatives in this application.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored niche: fusing learned optimization with second-order Quasi-Newton (SR1) structure, rather than the more common first-order learned optimizers.

The proposed secant-penalty-regularized, buffer-based rank-one construction (Eq. 7-9) is a reasonable and lightweight way to encourage PSD-ness and secant-condition compliance without the overhead of full matrix storage/inversion, and the authors show it empirically improves both convergence and cosine similarity to the Newton direction (Fig. 3a-b).

Evaluation spans multiple regimes: controlled quadratics, standard non-convex benchmark functions with performance profiles, and a real vision task (monocular HMR), which strengthens the case that the method is not overfit to one toy setting.

On HMR, the method attains lower PA-MPJPE than LGD with a notably smaller model (10.4M vs 17.4M params) and lower runtime/memory (Table 2), without dataset-specific fine-tuning, which is a meaningful practical advantage.

Reasonably thorough supplementary material: ablations over encoder inputs/hidden size, compute/memory profiling curves, qualitative HMR comparisons, and detailed hyperparameter tables support reproducibility.

Dimension-invariance design (element-wise learned modules) is a sensible and clearly stated design principle, and is at least partially validated by testing at dimensions different from training (N=2 train / N=10 test for quadratics; N=100 train / up to 1000 test for performance profiles).
weaknesses: The term 'learned projection' is somewhat misleading: Eq. (6)/(8) are stated as an argmin over a PSD matrix subject to a structural constraint, but in practice this is never solved explicitly — it is simply folded into the meta-training loss as a penalty term (Eq. 9). This is a soft training regularizer, not a genuine projection operator applied at inference, and the paper should be more precise about this distinction since it affects the theoretical soundness claims (PSD-ness during training is only encouraged, not guaranteed by an explicit projection step at test time beyond the structural form of Eq. 7).

HMR baselines are limited and somewhat dated (SMPLify 2016, SPIN 2019, LGD 2020); no comparison to more recent optimization- or regression-based SOTA methods mentioned in the related work (e.g., WHAM, PLIKS, PromptHMR), making the 'outperforms existing learned optimization-based approaches' claim narrower than the framing suggests.
Only PA-MPJPE is reported for HMR; other standard metrics (MPJPE, PVE) and variance/error bars across runs are absent, limiting confidence in the significance of the reported gains.

The initial quadratic experiment trains at N=2 and tests at N=10, which is a very low-dimensional toy setting for claims about dimension generalization; the more convincing generalization evidence (N=100 train, up to N=1000 test) is confined to the performance-profile experiment.

On the quadratic task, which is exactly the setting LBFGS is designed for, LBFGS still outperforms L-SR1 (Fig. 3a), somewhat undercutting the broader 'state-of-the-art performance' claim in the abstract/intro; this is acknowledged but the framing elsewhere is more triumphant than the results fully support.

Ablation results in Table 3 show configurations with heavily overlapping error bars (e.g., -2.51±2.64 vs -2.56±2.80), making it hard to conclude that the full input/hidden-size configuration is meaningfully better than several alternatives.

No formal convergence analysis or theoretical guarantee is provided for L-SR1 itself (only classical SR1/QN background is recapped in the appendix); the descent-direction guarantee (Lemma 1) is a restatement of a known result and does not establish that the learned components preserve this property beyond soft training incentives.
Code availability is only promised ('Code will be made publicly available') without a link or anonymized repository, which limits independent verification at review time.

The explanation for why LGD achieves lower 2D reprojection error but worse 3D accuracy (Fig. 4) — attributed to L-SR1 having 'better internalized 3D priors' — is speculative and not substantiated by further analysis or ablation isolating this claim.

strengths: Addresses an underexplored niche (learned second-order/quasi-Newton optimization) with a principled model-based deep learning design that embeds trainable rank-one updates inside the classical SR1 structure while preserving PSD-by-construction preconditioners.

The PGSM mechanism is a sensible, lightweight way to encourage secant consistency during meta-training without incurring an explicit projection subproblem at inference, and the paper provides a clear theoretical motivation (Eq. 6-9) connecting it to a least-squares PSD projection.

Extensive ablations are provided: buffer size sensitivity, cross-dimension generalization (N=2 to N=10), scalar vs. element-wise learning rates, encoder input/hidden-dimension ablations, and data-efficiency studies (training on fractions of AMASS) — these give useful insight into design choices and robustness.

Reasonably thorough reproducibility details: architecture tables, hyperparameter settings, and training protocols for each experiment are included in the appendix, along with runtime/memory profiling (Appendix A).

Real-world downstream evaluation on HMR (3DPW) shows the method outperforms the learned first-order baseline (LGD) and classical LBFGS/SPIN baselines with a smaller, more efficient model and no task-specific fine-tuning, which is a practically meaningful demonstration beyond toy benchmarks.
The limitations section is honest and specific about per-step cost, task-specific meta-training scope, and added hyperparameters.
weaknesses: The paper explicitly acknowledges that the composite update (PSD preconditioner combined with a per-coordinate learned learning-rate vector) is not guaranteed to be symmetric or to produce a descent direction, undermining the core theoretical selling point (PSD-by-construction) of the method; this gap is deferred entirely to empirical validation rather than resolved analytically.

The closest and most directly comparable prior work, the Transformer-based learned second-order optimizer of Gärtner et al. (2023), which is discussed extensively and contrasted conceptually throughout the paper (e.g., regarding naive vv^T PSD updates), is never empirically compared against in any experiment (quadratics, performance profiles, or HMR), leaving the central comparative claim (that PGSM improves over prior PSD-based learned second-order approaches) empirically unsupported.

On the very problem class SR1/QN methods are designed for (quadratics), classical LBFGS still outperforms L-SR1 with PGSM (Fig. 3a), which somewhat undercuts the practical value proposition of the learned approach for exactly the setting where second-order methods should excel; the advantage is confined to non-convex/diverse benchmark suites and the downstream HMR task.

Analytic experiments are trained and evaluated in fairly low dimensions (N=2 training, N=10 test for the core quadratic study), and cross-task generalization is not tested with a single unified model — each task family (quadratic, Rosenbrock, Rastrigin) requires separate meta-training, which limits the generality claims made in the introduction and conclusion.

Some reported comparisons rely on small differences that may not be statistically meaningful (e.g., Table 3 reports a 0.22mm PA-MPJPE difference between scalar and vector learning-rate variants) yet are used to support qualitative claims about coordinate-wise adaptation being beneficial for structured problems.

The project page/code link placeholder in the implementation section appears empty, raising concern about code availability and full reproducibility despite otherwise detailed hyperparameter reporting.

HMR results, while better than the learned-optimization baselines used, remain far behind modern regression-based SOTA (e.g., WHAM, PromptHMR), and while the paper reasonably frames this as a different efficiency/data regime, the practical significance of the accuracy gap relative to these methods is not fully contextualized.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored niche (learned second-order/quasi-Newton optimization) and proposes a reasonably clean idea: parameterize the preconditioner as B0 + sum of learned rank-one outer products (PSD by construction) and encourage secant consistency via a soft penalty rather than an explicit projection step at inference.

Fairly extensive set of controlled analytic experiments (quadratics, Rosenbrock, Rastrigin, performance profiles) that probe generalization across problem dimension and buffer size, plus several ablations (encoder inputs/hidden size, scalar vs. element-wise learning rate, limited-data training) in the appendix.

The HMR application is a sensible, practically motivated downstream task where reducing costly inner iterations matters; the method shows improved PA-MPJPE over the LGD baseline with a smaller model, lower runtime, and good data efficiency (competitive results even with 10% of AMASS).
Reasonable coverage of related work in learned optimization, quasi-Newton methods, and HMR, situating PGSM relative to prior PSD-via-vv^T approaches (e.g., Gärtner et al., 2023).
weaknesses: The paper's own analysis (Section 3.2/4) concedes that the PSD-by-construction preconditioner does not actually guarantee a descent direction once the coordinate-wise learning-rate factor is applied (the composite operator is not symmetric), which undercuts the central theoretical motivation for PGSM; the method's benefits are left to be justified purely empirically rather than through the promised structural guarantee.

The connection between the stated 'projection' formulation (Eqs. 6, 8) and the actual implementation is weak: no projection is ever solved, only a penalty term is added to the meta-loss, so calling the mechanism 'projection-guided' somewhat overstates the rigor of the approach relative to what is actually done.

Missing head-to-head comparison with the most directly relevant prior learned optimizer, the Transformer-based learned optimizer of Gärtner et al. (2023), which is repeatedly cited as the motivating 'naive fix' baseline (vv^T) but is never empirically compared against on the analytic benchmarks or HMR, despite being presented as the closest related work.

Evaluation scope is narrow relative to the broad claims in the abstract/intro about generalization to 'a broad range of iterative optimization problems': quadratics are tested only up to N=10 for the core generalization study, performance-profile dimensions are used mainly for timing/benchmarking rather than deep comparison with other learned optimizers, and only a single real-world application (HMR) is studied.

HMR comparisons mix methods trained on different data/architectures (Table 1 regression baselines marked with different training data), making some of the comparative claims about outperforming prior work less clean than presented; the main learned-optimization competitor (LGD) is from 2020, and no more recent learned-optimization HMR baselines are included.

The explicit disclaimer that L-SR1 is not intended as 'a drop-in optimizer for large-scale deep network training' substantially narrows the claimed significance relative to the framing in the introduction, which motivates the work by invoking the broader tension between end-to-end DL and classical optimization.

Presentation is dense with heavy notation and the paper would benefit from clearer, more direct articulation of exactly what guarantees (if any) hold for the method, given the acknowledged gap between the PSD construction and actual descent behavior.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored niche (learned second-order/quasi-Newton optimization) with a clear, well-motivated mechanism: PGSM constructs a PSD-by-construction rank-one preconditioner and uses a secant-violation penalty during meta-training, avoiding an explicit projection step at inference.

Experimental protocol is unusually thorough for a learned-optimizer paper: controlled quadratic studies isolating the effect of PGSM, cosine-similarity-to-Newton-direction analysis, dimension-generalization sweeps (N=2 to N=10), buffer-size robustness studies, and standard performance-profile benchmarking against L-BFGS/Adam/AdaHessian.

Good set of supporting ablations in the appendix: scalar vs. element-wise learning rates, encoder input/hidden-dim ablations, and a data-efficiency study showing L-SR1 trained on only 10% of AMASS still beats LGD trained on 100%.

Real downstream application (Monocular HMR) is a meaningful, high-dimensional, non-convex stress test with practical relevance, and the method is shown to be both more accurate and computationally cheaper (fewer params, lower runtime/memory) than the LGD baseline.

Honest and specific limitations discussion (per-step cost vs. first-order methods, meta-training task-distribution dependence, added hyperparameters), and the paper candidly notes in Section 3.2 that the coordinate-wise learning-rate map breaks the strict PSD-implies-descent guarantee, rather than overclaiming theoretical guarantees it cannot support.

Qualitative and quantitative HMR results (Fig. 5, 6, 7, Table 1) are consistent with the quantitative claims and provide a secant-consistency diagnostic (pose-block secant penalty) that directly supports the PGSM motivation.
weaknesses: The core theoretical motivation (Eq. 6-9) is heuristic: the paper motivates the secant penalty as being 'in the spirit of' a least-squares PSD projection, but never establishes that minimizing the proposed meta-training penalty actually approximates the true projection π+(Bk); this is asserted rather than proven, and the method's own text concedes the composite operator need not be symmetric, so the PSD-implies-descent argument does not formally transfer to the full update.

Baselines are somewhat dated/limited: on HMR, the only learned-optimization competitor is LGD (2020) and an ablated L-SR1 variant; other learned second-order optimizers discussed at length in Related Work (Gärtner et al. 2023 transformer-based optimizer, Li et al. 2020, Liao et al. 2023) are never empirically compared against, either on the analytic benchmarks or on HMR, despite being the most directly relevant prior art.

Reported HMR gains are numerically modest (51.74 vs. 55.90 mm PA-MPJPE vs. LGD; only 0.22 mm difference between element-wise vs. scalar learning-rate variants in Table 3), and no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals are given for the main HMR comparison in Table 1, making it hard to assess robustness of the claimed improvement.

Analytic benchmark suite is fairly narrow (quadratics, Rosenbrock, Rastrigin), and dimension-generalization claims rest on a fairly small sweep (train N=2, test N=10, or train N=100 and test up to 1000 in performance profiles) rather than a systematic study of how performance degrades with increasing dimensional gap.

The project/code URL referenced in the implementation details footnote appears to be missing or incomplete in the manuscript, raising a reproducibility concern given the many architectural and hyperparameter choices (buffer sizes, unroll depths, λsec, γ1/γ2) that would be needed to replicate results precisely.

Meta-training cost is substantial (400K iterations for HMR, ~15 hours per run for the analytic setup) and the paper does not report compute-matched comparisons against baselines (e.g., equivalent meta-training budget for LGD), leaving open whether gains stem from the method itself or from different effective training budgets.
